paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is a connective tissue disorder with features that overlap Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Reported features include aneurysms and dissections of the aorta and other arteries, mitral valve disease, craniofacial findings such as hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and cleft palate, and skeletal findings such as tall stature, arachnodactyly, kyphoscoliosis, and joint hypermobility (Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015; Kuechler et al., 2015). Variability within and between families is striking. Some affected individuals have no cardiovascular involvement, and 1 reported patient had growth retardation, low muscle mass, and distal arthrogryposis (Rienhoff et al., 2013).

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) described a European American girl, born to nonconsanguineous healthy parents, whom they followed to age 9 years. At birth she had distal arthrogryposis, with contractures of the right hand (most severe in the 3rd and 4th fingers) and of all toes. She also had mild hypotonia and a midline facial nevus flammeus. She had failure to thrive and delayed gross motor development, and at 17 months her weight was below the 1st centile. At that age she had hypertelorism, prominent eyes, blue sclerae, bifid uvula with an intact hard palate, mild retrognathia, a metopic ridge, pectus excavatum, pes planus, hyperextensible large joints, and markedly reduced subcutaneous fat. Muscle bulk was decreased, with low tone, diminished reflexes, and strength of 1/5. She stood independently at 20 months with a positive Gowers sign and walked at 24 months with a 'hip waddle' gait. Her neurocognitive development was normal. Radiographs showed bilateral coxa valga. At age 7 years her weight was still below the 1st centile, she had minimal subcutaneous fat, and her elbows and knees were markedly hyperextensible. A quadriceps biopsy at age 7 showed type 1 fiber predominance with mild focal fiber-type disproportion consistent with disuse, without dystrophic or inflammatory changes. Echocardiograms performed yearly from 18 months showed no cardiac defect, and aortic root dimensions were normal at 6.5 years.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with features overlapping Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Seven family members, aged 40 to 68 years, had aneurysms and dissections, mainly of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Three of them died from aortic dissection and rupture. Four members had mitral valve abnormalities, ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation that required surgery. Craniofacial features were subtle: long face, high-arched palate, and retrognathia. Other findings included pectus deformity, scoliosis, velvety skin, varices, and hiatal hernia, as well as autoimmune features (HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease, and celiac disease).

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) summarized 43 patients (23 male and 20 female; median age 34 years) from 11 families with TGFB3 mutations. Clinical overlap with Loeys-Dietz syndrome was significant, and variability within and between families was striking. Vascular involvement ranged from none at age 64 to type A dissection (median age 51 years), type B dissection (median age 44.5 years), abdominal aortic dissection, and death from cerebral aneurysm dissection at age 55. No patient had early dissection, dissection at a small aortic size, or striking arterial tortuosity. Other features included mitral valve disease and septal defects. Skeletal findings included tall stature (12 patients), arachnodactyly (16), kyphoscoliosis (11), joint hypermobility (9), and pectus deformity (8). Loeys-Dietz syndrome features included hypertelorism (14), bifid uvula (11), cleft palate (5), cervical spine instability, and clubfoot. No patient had ectopia lentis, and only 2 had early-onset osteoarthritis.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on a girl with low muscle mass, growth retardation, distal arthrogryposis, and features overlapping Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, and on her parents and 2 unaffected sibs. In the patient they found a de novo heterozygous mutation in the last exon of the TGFB3 gene (C409Y), and Sanger sequencing confirmed that it was de novo. The variant was absent from dbSNP130, the EVS database, and 1000 Genomes. The substituted cysteine is conserved across TGF-beta family ligands and is part of the 'cysteine knot' needed for ligand activity. In functional studies, the mutant ligand did not activate a TGF-beta reporter. In Xenopus embryos, coinjection of mutant and wildtype RNA reduced pSMAD2 and pERK1/2 signals, which suggested a dominant-negative effect. The patient also carried a second de novo heterozygous variant, a nonsense change in CDH2 (114020) (c.208C-T, Q70X). N-cadherin levels in her dermal fibroblasts did not differ significantly from those in controls, and Cdh2 heterozygous null mice are phenotypically normal. The authors therefore concluded that the CDH2 variant was unlikely to drive the phenotype, although they could not exclude a modifying effect.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of the Dutch family 1, sequencing of all known thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection (TAAD) genes found no causal mutation. Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) then identified a heterozygous splice site mutation in TGFB3 (c.754+2T-C) in the family. The mutation was absent from variant databases and segregated with the phenotype. cDNA sequencing showed skipping of exon 4, which results in an in-frame deletion of 36 amino acids. The same authors screened TGFB3 in 470 additional probands with syndromic or nonsyndromic TAAD, 350 by Sanger sequencing and 120 by exome sequencing. They found heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in 10 more probands: 4 missense mutations, 1 nonsense mutation, and 2 frameshift mutations. All of these mutations were absent from controls in EVS, 1000 Genomes, and Genome of the Netherlands. The missense mutations were D263H (family 3), R300W (families 2, 4, 5, and 11), I322T (family 10), and L401P (family 8). The other mutations were a de novo nonsense mutation, Y365X (family 6), and 2 single-base deletions causing frameshifts, L386RfsX21 (family 7) and N235MfsX11 (family 9). The proband in family 6 also carried a SMAD3 (603109) variant of unknown significance (A250T).
